title: Let's use our thinking caps!
author: Melissa Muth Martinez
summary: Melissa Muth Martinez argues that a good framework earns its keep only when it is applied practically, and she makes the case with Edward de Bono's Six Thinking Hats. She presents the hats as roles that a team can put on and take off, each one a deliberate mode of thinking rather than a personality trait. She lists settings where this helps, including change management, conflict resolution, decision-making, innovation and debriefs. She then walks through a partnership decision in which each person takes a different hat so the loudest voice does not drive the conversation. Her closing claim is that the structure diminishes ego because the point is to open minds rather than to be right. The piece is a short practitioner explainer and ends with a subscription pitch.
points: A framework is valuable to the degree that it can be applied, because it supplies structure and shared language when conversations spiral.
Each hat is a chosen angle of thinking (optimism, caution, process, facts, emotion, innovation), not a trait or a job, which is why people can swap them easily.
Assigning different hats in a group decision keeps the loudest or most urgent voice from dominating and brings the wider picture into view.
The method fits change management, conflict, decisions, innovation and retrospectives, and works by moving people from defensiveness to curiosity.
Thinking one hat at a time gives people permission not to know everything at once and weakens the role of ego.
quotes: They lend structure in the midst of spiraling conversations. They offer clear language when we’re unsure how to name things. They help us slow down and get centered around shared purpose when things feel fast or overwhelming.
The value of a hat as a symbol is that it indicates a role. Another advantage is that a hat can be put on or taken off with ease.
Each hat in the framework represents a particular mode of thinking. Not a personality trait, and definitely not a specific job—but a decision to think about a topic from a particular angle.
In many situations, the person with the loudest voice or most urgent concern might drive the whole conversation. But with the Six Thinking Hats, everyone tries on a different cap:
And just like that… everyone walks away not only having had the chance to have their unique perspectives heard, but with a better understanding of the bigger picture.

What I love about the Six Thinking Hats framework is that it gives us permission to not know everything at once. It’s honestly the most responsible thing to do, because it let’s people focus in on one thing at a time.
It’s a powerful tool for diminishing the power of the ego. Because it’s not about being right—it’s about opening up our minds to all the benefits of thinking.
